Madam Speaker, as I have listened to this debate today I keep going back in my mind to an experience I had about 10 years ago when I first took my three children out west to see the full breadth and scope of the country they were going to inherit. It was a trip filled with strikingly beautiful, impressive and marvellous experiences, but it was also a trip that involved some pretty devastating experiences.
Certainly one of those was travelling through B.C. and seeing what had been done to some of the mountainsides of the Rockies. To look up and see to a certain line a fabulous, wonderful forest growing there as it has been for many, many years, and then right beside it to see something that looked so devastated, so scarred, so out of keeping with anything that looked like human accomplishment. We saw huge amounts of wood left on the mountainside, we saw that somebody had just wrenched that whole mountainside apart without any care for what was being left behind and what would be there 10, 20 and
100 years from now. We saw the waste of an extremely valuable resource. It was a very sobering experience for all of us. We had a very thoughtful and sad dinner that evening as we talked about what was being done in parts of our country, a country that we felt were extremely valuable and deserved better.
At that time I was in municipal government and it made the things that I was concerned about seem relatively small. Yet I guess I have realized that in context every bit we do is important. Retaining a 100-acre conservation area in the middle of an urban municipality is an important contribution and insisting that windsurfers and boats use one side of a pier and not the other because on the other side the destruction of a wetlands area would be the result. All these things are small but important contributions.
Earlier last week I talked to a group of children at one of the schools in my riding. None of the children were more than 11 years old. They have spent the last year recycling paper because they understand, as some people in this House seem not to understand, that the preservation of trees is important. They know that the full tonne of paper that they have managed to recycle in the last year represents exactly 19 trees that did not get cut down.
It is amazing to think what a difference those small kinds of contributions could make right across the country. The children also understand what they have done and the importance of it in a much broader context because with the $50 that they earned from recycling that paper, they bought two acres of rain forest in the Amazon. They know that the forests and the trees are important, not only to the people who live in the Amazon but to all human beings on this earth. They know instinctively, but also intellectually because they have taken the time, as it seems some members of this House have not done, to understand what the balance of life in this world is all about. They know that as we are spewing carbon dioxide into the world, it is the natural areas, the growing areas of the world, that buffer the damage that is done by our abuse of the atmosphere. So they want to do their small part to protect what they can.
As the environment committee heard this year, they have learned that the burning of those forests and the destruction of those forests is destroying the long-term ability of a whole people to feed itself. As we heard this
February 1, 1990

morning, in 20 years, if the destruction of the rain forests proceeds as it is, there will be no soil and no ability for those people to feed themselves. That is pretty horrendous when you think about it; only 20 years from now. To me twenty years does not seem that long ago. In Brazil the ability of the people to feed themselves only 20 years from now is being destroyed on a daily basis and we are not doing anything about it.
The preservation of natural areas is an important issue world-wide, and it is an important issue in Canada. Again, we come to a question of balance. With governments it is always a question of balancing how much we use of resources with the need to ensure that they are there for the long term.
Any family understands this principle, understands that if you have so much money for groceries for the week you have to make it last for seven days. But we have never been able to translate that into an understanding of the world, an understanding that certain things do not simply replenish themselves when they are gone, and that if we want to continue enjoying the benefit of some of those resources we have to stage their use in a way that allows them to be replenished.
But there are some things on earth that are so precious, and certainly some things in our country that are so precious, that you cannot use them up or you will never be able to replace them. So it is a legacy that we owe to ourselves, to future generations, to preserve certain areas that are so unique that they are irreplaceable.
To find the balance is our job as politicians. What is the balance between the competing interests? Sometimes we have to be able to say, yes, jobs are important, but we cannot allow jobs to happen at the expense of destroying something that sustains life on this earth and that sustains the richness of our lives as human beings in this world.
In a way the argument is kind of ridiculous. I ask anybody just to picture a map of Canada. There is an ocean on either side and third one above us, and where do we live in this country? Nearly 80 per cent of us live in a little ribbon just so big. To say that we cannot look at that whole big area, more than half a continent, and set aside 12 per cent of its most precious areas so that it will be there in the future is simply not being realistic about
Government Orders
what this nation is all about. If we cannot do that now, we will never be able to do it.
Now is the time. We are on the threshold of the future of this country. We have just begun. This is the time to make a commitment and say that we want the most precious parts of this country to be forever a part of its heart, its soul and its physical existence. We will grow, we will expand and we will draw on the world's resources around those things which are too precious to use up, too precious to destroy. That still leaves us a whole huge country in which to do what we want to develop as human beings.
There are assets that have been here for millions of years. Who are we, in our small span on this earth, to say in our greed, our lack of caring and our need for immediate gratification, that we are going to take something that has been here for a million years and use it for our own short-term pleasure, denying it forever to other generations? Who are we to do that? What gives us the right?
Humanity walked out of the Garden of Eden, according to my religious tradition at least, and we like to think of that as something that happened at the beginning of the world. Well, in fact, it happened in the last small fraction of a percentage of world time. Who are we now to say that we are going to destroy the Gardens of Eden of our country or of our world?
I think the politicians are way behind the public. I think it is time we caught up with a public that is telling us, "We don't need disposable diapers if it means destroying forests, thank you very much". Instead of trailing that crowd, let us get in front of them and show some leadership.

Madam Speaker, I am very pleased to have the opportunity to join in the debate on this resolution here this afternoon.
Let me read the resolution again because it helps to focus on the debate if we refresh our minds. The motion moved by the member for Skeena states:
That, in the opinion of this House, the government should move to complete the national parks system (land and marine) by the year 2000 and should implement the recommendation of the World Commission on Environment and Development (Brundtland Report) that Canada protect at least 12 per cent of the land and marine zones.

February 1, 1990
Government Orders
I concur with the minister in that the government should take whatever steps are necessary to complete the country's system of terrestrial and marine parks. It is only by setting goals and a timetable in a strategic time path that we will accomplish these goals and make the achievement worth while.
Our 34 national parks are certainly vibrant, living museums ranging from the northern most areas of our country in the ice-covered tip of Ellesmere Island to the southern most marshes of Point Pelee, from the shores of the Pacific Rim on the west coast of British Columbia to those in eastern Canada at Terra Nova National Park in Nova Scotia.
I also agree that there is considerable urgency in this matter because forestry, hydroelectric power developments, mining and other resource extraction activities are steadily encroaching on Canada's last remaining wilderness.
The Minister of the Environment has already stated in this House, I believe on January 22, that he is personally committed to completing the system of national parks by the year 2000, and that he has directed his officials to prepare an action plan outlining how this ambitious and certainly important goal can be attained.
This commitment is a clear indication of the importance that the present government places on this activity and certainly we believe it is important to the people of Canada and to our country that we protect our environment and, in particular, some of these very important regions.
Each government of Canada owes it to the next to put its imprint on what is already the world's finest family of national parks. I am pleased that real progress has already been made by this government. The Minister of the Environment is giving it very high priority, also to creating new national parks. His short list of parks that are currently being seriously investigated in one way or another includes Banks Island, the northern Baffin Island, Bluenose Lake, the east arm of Great Slave Lake in the Northwest Territories and the Cape Churchill area in Manitoba.
I also agree with the House leader of the New Democratic Party that the government should work with some diligence to complete this national parks system. Canada is a country that has been shaped by water. We are bounded by water in many areas of our perimeter: the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence River along our
southern boundary; the Pacific Ocean on the west; the Arctic Ocean on the north; and, of course, the Atlantic on the east.
These water bodies have had a pronounced influence on our history. They continue and will always continue to have a major importance to our economy, not only from a tourism point of view, but also for the marine based industries.
Clearly the system of protected areas under the administration and control of the federal government will not be fully representative of Canada's geography until outstanding examples of these marine environments are set aside by the Parliament of Canada as future national marine parks are created under the National Parks Act.
I am proud that the government is also striving to complete the network of national marine parks in a systematic and timely manner. This is a policy that is in place and it is a guide to the selection, establishment, planning and management of new marine parks. Similar to our national terrestrial parks, there are 29 various marine regions that have been adopted in setting the scope of this particular system. The long-term goal is to provide adequate representation of each of these 29 marine regions in the marine park system.
However, I cannot support the member's contention that the government should complete the network of national marine parks in this very short timeframe, which is really just this next decade. It would be an admirable goal, but I suspect it is something that is unattainable. I think we should most certainly have to move onward with the job. Of course there are several reasons to move on, but there are also reasons why I think we have to proceed with, at least, some caution.
First, the creation of national marine parks is still in its infancy and the national marine parks policy which sets aside the stage of selecting, establishing, managing our marine parks in Canada was first approved by the former Minister of Environment in September 1986 under the direction of this current government.
The following year, a provision to create a national marine park in the waters surrounding South Moresby National Park reserve by the year 1993 was included in the park agreement between Canada and British Columbia. Legislative authority for the government to create national marine parks in general, as a separate type of park and to proclaim the Fathom Five in Georgian Bay,

Ontario, which is not too distant from my riding, as Canada's first such park was passed in 1988.
The point I wish to make in this brief chronology of events, is that things are moving fairly rapidly on this front. Research, planning, support for new marine parks must accompany the establishment of such parks. In my opinion, the government would be wise to proceed with the maximum swiftness that can be attained, but certainly with some caution as well in the creation of these national parks so we do it well and we learn the proper protection of these marine reserves, how to make opportunities for people to go into these areas, but to do it in a safe and conservation-minded way.
I suppose we might say that hiking boots and backpacks must give way to swimming fins and scuba tanks in some of these areas. It will be interesting and certainly very enjoyable for all Canadians to see the marine park group continue to expand.
Because marine ecosystems differ significantly from those on land, the experience gained from managing the country's century old national park systems are not readily transferable to the marine park counterparts. Furthermore, the experiences of other countries in dealing with marine parks are not always directly transferable because there are relatively few examples where marine parks have been established in cold or temperate and Arctic oceans which are the sorts of waters that surround our country.
There is another important reason for questioning the haste that is included. I do not question that we must move forward, and move forward as swiftly as possible, but I think establishing all these marine parks by the year 2000, within one decade, is a little bit bigger challenge than one can expect in order to proceed in an organized way.
As I mentioned earlier there is only one marine park in the country at this time. It was established in 1988. I mentioned one in South Moresby in British Columbia. That really means two df the 29 regions have so far been represented, leaving 27 regions yet unrepresented. If the government were to move forward and follow the timetable suggested by the hon. member, it would mean establishing an average of two to three marine parks per

year over the next 10 years. Although it may be something that we would like to talk about, I suspect that goal is unrealistic.
In my view, the government should aim to establish at least two national marine parks in each of Canada's three environments and on the Great Lakes by the year 2000. This would mean that within 10 years there would be a total of no fewer than eight national marine parks. Work towards this goal has already begun. For example, the Minister of Environment is negotiating with the province of Quebec now for the establishment of a marine park at the Saguenay River. This is an area of considerable diversity and species. Of course, the ones of particular interest are the blue whale and the beluga whale.
Park officials are also examining the prospects of a new marine park in three northern regions. Those are the Lancaster Sound area at the eastern end of the Northwest Passage, the Hudson Bay and along the coast of Labrador. Similar studies will be undertaken this year in other marine areas if sufficient resources are available.
I think this goal is both realistic and wise in the view of the newness of the marine system. Also I think it provides those with the responsibilities of managing these new underwater parks an opportunity to develop their expertise, develop policies and correct any problems that may develop in the establishment of these parks.
The new national marine parks will also serve to increase public awareness of the benefits of marine parks and to help develop stronger public support for this new initiative. With the experience thus gained and the strong public support that already has been generated, Canada will have a solid basis by the year 2000 for a national marine park system that will match the grandeur that is internationally recognized for our current terrestrial parks.
Madam Speaker, I differ from some of those who have been critical of the government today. We have made significant headway on the terrestrial parks and more negotiations are going on and others will start in the not too distant future. There is significant progress in our marine park system which was just recently started by this government.

I look forward with eagerness, along with a great many Canadians, to see our fantastic family of national parks grow in the future. I am sure, as I stand here today, that there will be many new parks by the year 2000.

Madam Speaker, I appreciate many of the remarks that were just made by the member who just spoke. I am sure he is aware that there are 39 bioregions in the country and there are park representations in 21 of those bioregions at a rate of about one and a half parks per bioregion, because we have 34 national parks.
When the minister was speaking this morning, he indicated that the plan of the government right now is to simply have one representative area in each of the bioregions that are left, although if we were to proceed as we have to date, we could in fact suggest that there is a need for 27 terrestrial national parks as well as for 27 national marine parks.
But the point that the members seem to be driving at is that there simply is not time between now and the year 2000 to complete the system either due to time, money, political will or everything else. I suggest the members go back and look at the 1987 task force recommendations on national park establishment because they made it quite clear that we will have foregone the opportunity to have made a lot of decisions if we dilly-dally very many more years, even into this decade.
A very strong recommendation was made by a number of groups that I have referred to earlier in my speech about the need simply to establish the protected areas. As they said:
Establishing protected areas need not be an expensive undertaking, especially if the goal is to reserve lands and waters primarily on crown land over the next 10 years, leaving the "development" of services for the future.
They are basically indicating two competing interests for those areas, that these are areas of national significance either for biological reasons or biodiversity reasons. Would not the members support and endorse the idea that we need to complete the designation and the reserving of those 27 marine areas during this decade as well as those 18 to 27 national terrestrial areas, because if we do not, we will have foregone the opportunity?

Madam Speaker, I certainly cannot disagree with the general objective that the member mentions. I think the problem with urgency, of course, as the member is well aware, is that there are other interested parties in all of these areas, governments and various other groups who claim their own interests for whatever reasons in the important terrestrial and marine areas of our country.
While each group has its own good intentions, it does require a great deal of time to negotiate these agreements. Even to put some sort of restriction on prior to significant negotiation, it is not all that easy to accomplish this in certain areas, as the member is well aware. We have situations going on in our country right now where there has been various development or control agreements on sensitive areas.
I think of the situation in areas like Temagami where there has been a longstanding agreement of many years that is under reconsideration. Of course, there is relatively little agreement on how that should be handled. It has developed into a very controversial issue in that area. So even to say that we can set aside a certain area that we would like to have for a national park somewhere in the future, and that we might start serious negotiations four or five years down the road, it will also be met with significant objection.
I think as resources and time is available, it is important that we look into these situations. I have confidence that the minister will do that because if we just look back we will see the progress that has been made in the last five years.
